raw_case_text:
A 75-year-old male patient was referred to our emergency department by a private physician with a provisional diagnosis of acute febrile illness with lower respiratory tract infection and bilateral pneumonia, along with severe hypoxia. The patient had been experiencing fever and shortness of breath for one month on-and-off basis, with cough and weakness. He had a known case of type 2 diabetes mellitus and epilepsy and was on treatment for the same. He was a non-smoker, non-alcoholic, and not hypertensive. There was no history of pulmonary tuberculosis, and he was a shopkeeper by profession.
On examination, the patient was conscious and oriented to time, place, and person. He was tachypneic and dyspneic, with a blood pressure of 121/86 mmHg, pulse rate of 92/minute, and respiratory rate of 25/minute. His SPO2 was 85% in room air. Bilateral rhonchi and crepitations were heard on auscultation of the chest, and bilateral pedal edema was also present. The patient was started on non-invasive ventilation.
The total leucocyte count was 13,770/muL, differential leucocyte count - neutrophil (95.3%) and lymphocytes (2.1%), and hemoglobin was 10.8 g/dL. X-ray PA view showed bilateral nodular opacities and infiltrates, along with areas of consolidation (Figure 1).
HRCT of the chest shows multiple centrilobular nodules and multiple heterogeneously enhancing lesions of bilateral lung fields with consolidation of the right lower lobe (Figure 2).
Sputum and blood cultures were sent, and the patient was started empirically on IV meropenem 1 g TID and IV clarithromycin 500 mg BD. The patient's condition was deteriorating, and the medical team planned to put him on a ventilator. However, the patient's attenders refused and decided to take discharge against medical advice on the second day of admission.
Sputum samples were sent for microbiological examination, and on Gram stain, Gram-positive beaded branching filamentous bacilli were seen (Figure 3).
The modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain (1% H2SO4) from the sample demonstrated pink-colored beaded branching acid-fast filamentous bacilli suggestive of Nocardia species (Figure 4).
After 48 hours of incubation, no pathogenic microorganisms could be isolated from the sputum culture. The blood culture was negative after incubation for five days. A 10% potassium hydroxide mount (KOH) showed no fungal elements. M. tuberculosis complex was not detected by cartridge-based nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT) of sputum.
In the culture of sputum, Nocardia could not be isolated after 72 hours of incubation of Sabouraud's dextrose agar (SDA) and blood agar. However, Nocardia spp. was detected by direct microscopy, and the treating doctor was informed. Unfortunately, by that time, the patient had left the hospital against medical advice. When the medical team tried to contact the patient directly, the patient's relative informed them that the patient had died the next day after being discharged from the hospital. The sample was subjected to 16S rRNA sequencing and identified as N. wallacei (GenBank accession number: OR533615).
Antimicrobial susceptibility testing was not done as Nocardia could not be isolated in culture.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 75-year-old male presented with a 1-month history of intermittent fever, shortness of breath, cough, and generalized weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient experienced on-and-off fever and shortness of breath for 1 month accompanied by cough and weakness, and was referred to the emergency department by a private physician with acute febrile lower respiratory tract infection, bilateral pneumonia, and severe hypoxia.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of type 2 diabetes mellitus and epilepsy on treatment. Shopkeeper by profession; non-smoker, non-alcoholic, non-hypertensive, and no history of pulmonary tuberculosis.
subjective.review_of_systems: On maintenance medications for type 2 diabetes mellitus and epilepsy.

objective.physical_examination: Conscious and oriented to time, place, and person, but tachypneic and dyspneic: BP 121/86 mmHg, pulse 92/min, respiratory rate 25/min, and SpO2 85% on room air. Chest auscultation revealed bilateral rhonchi and crepitations, and bilateral pedal edema was present.
objective.routine_investigations: CBC showed leukocytosis with total leukocyte count 13,770/uL (neutrophils 95.3%, lymphocytes 2.1%) and hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL. Chest X-ray (PA view) demonstrated bilateral nodular opacities, infiltrates, and areas of consolidation. Blood culture (5 days), sputum 10% KOH mount, and sputum CBNAAT for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest HRCT revealed multiple centrilobular nodules and multiple heterogeneously enhancing lesions across bilateral lung fields with right lower lobe consolidation. Antimicrobial susceptibility testing could not be performed because the organism did not grow on Sabouraud dextrose agar or blood agar after 72 hours.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Pulmonary nocardiosis caused by Nocardia wallacei was confirmed via direct sputum microscopy—which demonstrated Gram-positive beaded branching filamentous bacilli on Gram stain and pink beaded branching acid-fast filamentous bacilli on modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain (1% H2SO4)—and 16S rRNA gene sequencing (GenBank OR533615). The patient was initially managed with non-invasive ventilation and empirical IV meropenem (1 g TID) plus IV clarithromycin (500 mg BD). Due to clinical deterioration requiring invasive mechanical ventilation, his family took discharge against medical advice on hospital day 2 before microbiological confirmation arrived, and the patient died the following day.
